Key Research Thinking Patterns: Machine Learning-Driven Spatial Heterogeneity Analysis: Employing ensemble learning algorithms (XGBoost, Random Forest) coupled with SHAP interpretability to quantify non-linear relationships between urban form, landscape metrics, and Land Surface Temperature (LST), identifying specific cooling/warming thresholds (e.g., vegetation diversity >0.65) within Local Climate Zones.

Multi-Scale LST Downscaling and Bias Correction: Utilizing Radiative Transfer Equations (RTE) and machine learning models to downscale coarse-resolution satellite data (e.g., MODIS/VIIRS) to high-resolution (10-30m) to accurately assess micro-scale urban cooling effects, correcting systematic overestimations of park cooling efficiency in low-resolution datasets.

Unsupervised Computer Vision for Object Detection: Developing novel, non-deep learning algorithms (combining Gradient Difference Window Detection, Double Ring Sliding Detection, and Adaptive Iterative Erosion) to extract individual tree structures from sub-meter RGB imagery, enabling large-scale, computationally efficient monitoring of agricultural and forest resources without extensive labeled data.

Global Comparative Spatial Statistics: Applying Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) and correlation analyses to geostationary satellite-derived Thermal Condition Indices across thousands of cities to map global spatial heterogeneity in urban heat stress and identify dominant topographic versus socioeconomic drivers.
Summary Description: Xiangming Xiao is a principal investigator specializing in urban climatology, remote sensing, and geographic information systems, with a focus on urban heat island (UHI) mitigation and sustainable urban planning. His research integrates high-resolution satellite data (Landsat, Sentinel, ECOSTRESS) with advanced machine learning frameworks (XGBoost-SHAP, Random Forest) to analyze the spatial heterogeneity of urban thermal environments. Key contributions include developing methods to downscale LST for accurate park cooling assessment, identifying critical thresholds in urban form and greenspace morphology for heat regulation, and creating unsupervised computer vision algorithms for large-scale agricultural monitoring. His work bridges technical geospatial analysis with translational goals in public health, climate adaptation, and policy formulation, aiming to optimize green infrastructure and reduce heat-related mortality risks in rapidly urbanizing regions.
